market_scan.market_size_text: The buyer pool is the industrial microwave heating equipment industry itself: ~$1.4-1.6B/yr equipment sales (2025) carried by a few dozen established OEMs plus a long tail of regional/tunnel-machine builders. The comparable software market — electromagnetic simulation software overall — is ~$1.5-2.9B/yr growing 10-18%/yr, but the microwave-heating slice of that is tiny (order ~$30-80M/yr), because today it is served as a byproduct of general EM tools. A purpose-built applicator/cavity design tool addresses this niche plus the currently unmonetized 'in-house code + trial-and-error' segment.

regions.Europe: ~$0.4-0.5B (densest OEM cluster: Germany/France/Italy/UK; European leaders ~35-40% of global microwave-dryer share)
regions.Asia: ~$0.5-0.6B (largest regional equipment market ~35%; many mid/low-tier machine builders in China/Japan/India)
regions.Africa: ~$0.05-0.15B (incl. Middle East; small OEM presence, mostly import market)

market_scan.target_customers_text: A concentrated, easy-to-map customer set: roughly 15-25 established industrial microwave OEMs (Muegge, Püschner, Sairem, Linn High Therm, Industrial Microwave Systems, Ferrite/Microwave Techniques, AMTek, Thermex, Cellencor, plus generator/component vendors like Richardson, CPI, e2v, Hitachi, Toshiba), ~30-80 mid-size specialists, and a long tail of ~100-300 smaller/regional tunnel-equipment builders concentrated in Asia. They are reachable through a handful of channels (AMPERE, IMPI conferences, trade fairs), and each has an engineering department that already understands the problem — the best-defined customer group of the three hypotheses, but also the smallest.
market_scan.players_text: The design-simulation market is dominated by general-purpose EM suites: Ansys HFSS, Dassault CST Studio Suite, Altair FEKO, COMSOL Multiphysics+RF together take ~70-80% of EM-simulation spend (top-5 CAE vendors hold ~2/3 of the ~$10B CAE market). These tools were built for telecom/electronics, so microwave-heating workflows (temperature-dependent dielectrics, moving loads, thermal runaway, calorimetric power balance) must be rebuilt by each OEM's engineers. Only one small vendor (QWED, Poland, QuickWave) sells heating-dedicated modules; the rest of the niche is in-house codes, consultancies and academia — the market is effectively one strong incumbent category plus one proven niche precedent.
players: Large (Ansys/Synopsys HFSS, Dassault SIMULIA CST, Altair FEKO/HyperWorks, COMSOL RF, Keysight)
general 3D EM solvers with optional thermal coupling; pricing ~$10k (COMSOL) to ~$50k+ (HFSS) per seat
Medium (QWED QuickWave, Remcom XFdtd, IMST Empire)
specialist FDTD tools; only QuickWave offers a dedicated microwave-heating module
Small (open-source openEMS/MEEP, in-house OEM codes, MW design consultancies, university groups)
free/expert tools and bespoke simulation services filling gaps the suites leave
regulation: Safety requirements for industrial microwave heating installations (leakage, interlocks, emission limits 800 MHz-6 GHz ISM); design-stage simulation of leakage and hot spots directly supports conformity
RF emission limits for ISM equipment; applicator/cavity design determines compliance, so simulation that predicts emissions shortens certification cycles
Equipment must operate inside ISM allocations (915 MHz mainly Americas, 2.45/5.8 GHz worldwide, plus national variants like 896 MHz UK/922 MHz JP); multi-band-aware design tools cover export markets
Minimum worker EMF-exposure requirements influence applicator shielding/feeder design — a simulation output OEMs must document
US rules for ISM equipment emissions; required for machines exported to the largest single market

technologies.name: Full-wave 3D EM + thermal multiphysics suites (Ansys HFSS, CST Studio Suite, COMSOL RF+Heat Transfer, Altair FEKO)
technologies.how: FEM (HFSS, COMSOL) or FIT/FDTD (CST) solvers compute cavity fields; coupled thermal/CFD step converts dissipated power into temperature fields; engineers script parametric sweeps and optimization manually.
technologies.performance: Experimentally validated against real applicators (e.g., 915 MHz single-mode applicator benchmark COMSOL vs CST); single runs minutes-hours; full design-space sweeps days-weeks on workstations
technologies.limits: Built for antennas/PCB/radar, not heating: temperature-dependent dielectrics, moving loads and runaway need manual coupling; steep learning curve; ~$10-70k per seat; results highly sensitive to dielectric input data the OEM must measure itself

technologies.name: Microwave-heating-dedicated FDTD (QWED QuickWave + Basic Heating Module, QW-OptimiserPlus)
technologies.how: FDTD EM-thermal co-simulation with temperature-/enthalpy-dependent media, moving/rotating load support, source-frequency tuning and built-in optimizer — the closest existing product to the H4 idea.
technologies.performance: Purpose-built features cut model-building effort vs generalists; validated in high-temperature processing studies (e.g., zirconia sintering, runaway prediction); niche vendor scale
technologies.limits: Small company with limited marketing reach, ecosystem and multiphysics breadth; still requires expert users and measured dielectric data; little traction outside the specialist MW-heating community

technologies.name: Analytical/mode-matching and reduced-order cavity models + in-house codes
technologies.how: Modal analysis of canonical applicator geometries, equivalent-circuit load models, and OEM-specific empirical design rules accumulated over decades.
technologies.performance: Seconds per evaluation; adequate for early sizing of single-mode applicators and waveguide feeds; embedded in OEM know-how
technologies.limits: Fails for multimode cavities, irregular loads and coupled thermal behavior — exactly where expensive mistakes happen; knowledge is tribal, undocumented, and non-transferable

technologies.name: Build-and-test prototyping (calorimetry, thermography, product trials)
technologies.how: The incumbent workflow: fabricate applicator variants, measure field/temperature indirectly, iterate in the pilot plant.
technologies.performance: Highest fidelity for final validation; typical industrial applicator prototypes cost order ~$50-500k and add weeks-months per iteration
technologies.limits: Slow, expensive, and blind to internal EM fields (only surface temperature/leakage measurable); limits the design space an OEM can explore; scales poorly with custom-machine business

technologies.name: AI/surrogate-assisted EM optimization
technologies.how: Train surrogate models on solver results to explore large design spaces; emerging feature in vendor roadmaps (Ansys optiSLang-type, CST+SIMULIA AI).
technologies.performance: Market analyses report AI surrogates cutting multi-day solver campaigns to hours; adopted in antenna/radar design first
technologies.limits: Needs hundreds-thousands of training simulations and curated dielectric data — expensive to bootstrap; no microwave-heating-specific surrogate libraries exist today

technologies.name: Dielectric property measurement (cavity perturbation, coaxial probe, resonant methods)
technologies.how: Laboratory characterization of complex permittivity vs temperature/frequency/moisture — the mandatory input for every heating simulation.
technologies.performance: Well-established methods; published comparisons show strong sensitivity of simulated temperature to dielectric accuracy; ProSeed could own a proprietary materials database
technologies.limits: Data is scattered, mostly unpublished, and must often be re-measured per customer material — a structural bottleneck no solver vendor solves

tech_baseline.why_better_text: Generalist suites sell OEMs an expensive, expert-only toolkit and leave each manufacturer to re-implement microwave-heating physics — dielectric databases, moving-load handling, calorimetric power balance, runaway prediction — on top of $50k seats. A domain-focused design tool can win by shipping applicator/cavity templates, a proprietary temperature-dependent dielectric library, and built-in ISM/emission checks, collapsing model-building time from engineer-weeks to days and making optimization loops practical for mid-size OEMs that cannot justify HFSS specialists. QWED's QuickWave proves a niche product can exist; ProSeed's advantage over QWED is owning real equipment design + process data, and offering it as tool-plus-service where incumbents sell seats alone.
key_assumptions: Only ~15-25 established OEMs plus ~100-300 smaller builders exist globally, so reachable customers number in the low hundreds — a niche that caps license revenue but suits focused B2B sales (assumed; consistent with market reports naming ~10-20 key players)
Generalist EM seats cost ~$10k (COMSOL base+RF ~EUR 7.7k) to ~$50-70k (HFSS) before the expert labor to use them (measured, public price lists/forums)
OEM design today still relies heavily on iterative prototyping at ~$50-500k per applicator iteration (assumed, industry-typical for custom RF hardware)
Accurate results require measured temperature-dependent dielectric data per product — whoever owns that data owns simulation accuracy (measured, applicator validation literature)
A specialist tool must be ~5-10x faster to a manufacturable design than the generalist workflow to overcome switching inertia (assumed)
